items.readable_text:
Content:
If an [MATH: n\!\times \!n] matrix [MATH: A] has an entire row or column of zeros, then its determinant is equal to zero.

Content:
For example, consider the matrix [MATH: A] given below:

Content:
[MATH: [∗|∗|∗; 0|0|0; ∗|∗|∗]]

Content:
The second row consists of all zeros, and the asterisks ([MATH: \ast]) may represent any number.

Content:
Let's compute the determinant using the Laplace expansion across the second row:

Content:
[MATH: det(A)|=|∗|∗|∗; 0|0|0; ∗|∗|∗|; = (− 1)^{2 + 1}(0)|∗|∗; ∗|∗|+ (− 1)^{2 + 2}(0)|∗|∗; ∗|∗|+ (− 1)^{2 + 3}(0)|∗|∗; ∗|∗|; = 0 + 0 + 0; = 0]

Content:
Notice that it doesn't matter what numbers are represented by the asterisks ([MATH: \ast]). Each cofactor is multiplied by zero, so the final result must be zero.

items.readable_text:
Content:
Now, suppose a matrix has no zero rows but it has two identical rows:

Content:
[MATH: [1|2|1; 1|2|3; 1|2|1]]

Content:
We can subtract the [MATH: 1]st row from the [MATH: 3]rd row, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: A|= [1|2|1; 1|2|3; 1|2|1]|R_{3}|:=R_{3} + (− 1)R_{1}; ∼[1|2|1; 1|2|3; 0|0|0]; = B]

Content:
Since this operation does not change the determinant, we get [MATH: \det(A) = \det(B).] Furthermore, as [MATH: B] contains a zero row, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: \det(A) = \det(B) = 0.]

Content:
Notice that we can use this method with columns too. Therefore, we have the following property:

Content:
> If a square matrix has at least two identical rows/columns, its determinant equals zero.

[MATH: [4|sqrt(13)|4; 4|11|4; sqrt(3)|9|sqrt(3)]]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's examine each matrix in turn.

  • Since [MATH: A] has two identical columns, we obtain [MATH: [4|sqrt(13)|4; 4|11|4; sqrt(3)|9|sqrt(3)]]

  • Since [MATH: B] is a diagonal matrix, its determinant is given by the product of the elements of the main diagonal: [MATH: \det(B) = 3 \cdot (-4) \cdot (-2) = 24]

Therefore, [MATH: 5\det(A)-\det(B) = 5 \cdot 0 - 24 = -24.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
In conclusion, if an [MATH: n\!\times \!n] matrix [MATH: A] satisfies any one of the following conditions, then [MATH: \det(A)=0.]

Content:
1. [MATH: A] has a zero row/column
2. [MATH: A] has two identical rows/columns
3. [MATH: A] has two proportional rows/columns
4. [MATH: A] has a row/column that is a linear combination of other rows/columns

Content:
Notice that condition IV encompasses each of the conditions I, II, and III. If we have a zero row/column, two identical rows/columns, or proportional rows/columns, then the rows/columns form a linearly dependent set of vectors.
In turn, this means that one of the rows/columns is a linear combination of other rows/columns.

Content:
Watch out! While all of the above conditions are sufficient to conclude that [MATH: \det(A)=0,] only condition IV is necessary to conclude that [MATH: \det(A)=0.]
In other words, if we have a matrix [MATH: A] with [MATH: \det(A)=0,] then conditions I, II, and III may or may not be satisfied, while condition IV must be satisfied.

Content:
So, we have the following theorem:

Content:
> [MATH: \det(A)=0] if and only if one of the rows/columns of [MATH: A] is a linear combination of other rows/columns of [MATH: A.]

Content:
Finally, note also that in the case of a [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix only, statements III and IV mean the same thing.

Content:
Geometrically, the absolute value of an [MATH: n \times n] determinant can be interpreted as the volume of the [MATH: n]-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the columns of the determinant.

Content:
For example:

Content:
- Suppose the columns of a [MATH: 3\times 3] matrix [MATH: A] are [MATH: {\color{black}\mathbf{a}}, {\color{black}\mathbf{b}},] and [MATH: {\color{black}\mathbf{c}}.]
[MATH: [|||||; a|b|c;|||||]]
The [MATH: 3]-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the columns of [MATH: A] is depicted below:

[IMG: /graphics/2dd6c41a3db7336520a034a51b742bbb]

The volume [MATH: V] of this parallelepiped equals the absolute value of the determinant of [MATH: A{:}]
[MATH: V = \left|\det(A)\right|]
- Now suppose the columns of a [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix [MATH: B] are [MATH: {\color{black}\mathbf{p}}] and [MATH: {\color{black}\mathbf{q}}.]
[MATH: [|||; p|q;|||]]
The [MATH: 2]-dimensional parallelepiped (i.e., the parallelogram) spanned by vectors [MATH: \mathbf{p}] and [MATH: \mathbf{q}] is shown below:

[IMG: /graphics/47c3f62329b5f9c05401af301b3d2660]

The two-dimensional volume [MATH: V] (i.e., the area) of this parallelepiped equals the absolute value of the determinant of [MATH: B{:}]
[MATH: V = \left|\det(B)\right|]
- In general, the absolute value of the determinant of an [MATH: n\times n] matrix [MATH: M] gives the [MATH: n]-dimensional volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the columns of [MATH: M.]

Content:
In this lesson, we studied the following property:

Content:
> [MATH: \det(A) = 0] if and only if one of the columns of [MATH: A] is a linear combination of other columns of [MATH: A].

Content:
What does this property mean in geometric terms?

Content:
The component [MATH: \det(A) = 0] implies that the [MATH: n]-dimensional parallelepiped formed by the columns of [MATH: A] has zero volume. Conversely, when one of the columns of [MATH: A] is a linear combination of other columns, it indicates that the corresponding parallelepiped possesses at most [MATH: n-1] distinct dimensions.

Content:
Consider the following examples:

Content:
- In the case of a [MATH: 3]-dimensional parallelepiped, if the vector [MATH: \mathbf{c}] is a linear combination of the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}], then [MATH: \mathbf{c}] lies within the plane containing [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}]. In other words, the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}], [MATH: \mathbf{b}], and [MATH: \mathbf{c}] are coplanar. Consequently, we obtain a "flat" ([MATH: 2]-dimensional) figure with a volume of [MATH: 0].
- For the parallelogram example, if the vector [MATH: \mathbf{q}] is a linear combination of the vector [MATH: \mathbf{p}] (i.e., [MATH: \mathbf{p}] and [MATH: \mathbf{q}] are proportional), then [MATH: \mathbf{q}] resides on the line containing vector [MATH: \mathbf{p}]. In other words, the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{p}] and [MATH: \mathbf{q}] are collinear. This results in a [MATH: 1]-dimensional object with a [MATH: 2]-dimensional volume (i.e., area) of [MATH: 0].

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
If an [MATH: n\!\times \!n] matrix [MATH: A] has an entire row or column of zeros, then its determinant is equal to zero.

Content:
For example, consider the matrix [MATH: A] given below:

Content:
[MATH: [∗|∗|∗; 0|0|0; ∗|∗|∗]]

Content:
The second row consists of all zeros, and the asterisks ([MATH: \ast]) may represent any number.

Content:
Let's compute the determinant using the Laplace expansion across the second row:

Content:
[MATH: det(A)|=|∗|∗|∗; 0|0|0; ∗|∗|∗|; = (− 1)^{2 + 1}(0)|∗|∗; ∗|∗|+ (− 1)^{2 + 2}(0)|∗|∗; ∗|∗|+ (− 1)^{2 + 3}(0)|∗|∗; ∗|∗|; = 0 + 0 + 0; = 0]

Content:
Notice that it doesn't matter what numbers are represented by the asterisks ([MATH: \ast]). Each cofactor is multiplied by zero, so the final result must be zero.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Determinants with Identical Rows or Identical Columns

Content:
Now, suppose a matrix has no zero rows but it has two identical rows:

Content:
[MATH: [1|2|1; 1|2|3; 1|2|1]]

Content:
We can subtract the [MATH: 1]st row from the [MATH: 3]rd row, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: A|= [1|2|1; 1|2|3; 1|2|1]|R_{3}|:=R_{3} + (− 1)R_{1}; ∼[1|2|1; 1|2|3; 0|0|0]; = B]

Content:
Since this operation does not change the determinant, we get [MATH: \det(A) = \det(B).] Furthermore, as [MATH: B] contains a zero row, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: \det(A) = \det(B) = 0.]

Content:
Notice that we can use this method with columns too. Therefore, we have the following property:

Content:
> If a square matrix has at least two identical rows/columns, its determinant equals zero.

---

Item 3 — Example: Calculating the Determinant of a Matrix With A Zero Row/Column or Two Identical Rows/Columns

Example Prompt:
Find [MATH: 5\det(A)-\det(B),] where
[MATH: [4|sqrt(13)|4; 4|11|4; sqrt(3)|9|sqrt(3)]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's examine each matrix in turn.

- Since [MATH: A] has two identical columns, we obtain
[MATH: [4|sqrt(13)|4; 4|11|4; sqrt(3)|9|sqrt(3)]]

- Since [MATH: B] is a diagonal matrix, its determinant is given by the product of the elements of the main diagonal:
[MATH: \det(B) = 3 \cdot (-4) \cdot (-2) = 24]

Therefore, [MATH: 5\det(A)-\det(B) = 5 \cdot 0 - 24 = -24.]

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: Determinants with Proportional Rows/Columns

Content:
Now, suppose a matrix has no zero rows and no identical rows but it has two proportional rows:

Content:
[MATH: [1|2|1; 1|2|3; − 3|− 6|− 3]]

Content:
We can add three times the [MATH: 1]st row to the [MATH: 3]rd row, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: A|= [1|2|1; 1|2|3; − 3|− 6|− 3]|R_{3}|:=R_{3} + 3R_{1}; ∼[1|2|1; 1|2|3; 0|0|0]; = B]

Content:
Since this operation does not change the determinant, we get [MATH: \det(A) = \det(B).] Furthermore, as [MATH: B] contains a zero row, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: \det(A) = \det(B) = 0.]

Content:
Notice that we can use this method with columns too. Therefore, we have the following property:

Content:
> If a square matrix has at least two proportional rows/columns, its determinant equals zero.

---

Item 7 — Example: Calculating the Determinant of a Matrix With Two Proportional Rows/Columns

Example Prompt:
Which of the following determinants are equal to [MATH: 0?]

[MATH: 2|sqrt(3)|1; 1|1|2; 3|3|6]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's examine each of the given determinants in turn.

- The matrix [MATH: A] has proportional rows:
[MATH: [2|sqrt(3)|1; 1|1|2; 3|3|6]]
As a result, [MATH: |A| = 0.]
- The matrix [MATH: B] is a triangular matrix, so
[MATH: |B| = (-1) \cdot 4 \cdot (-3) = 12 \neq 0.]
- The matrix [MATH: C] has a zero row:
[MATH: [− 1|sqrt(2)|sqrt(3); 0|0|0; 1|0|− 1]]
As a result, [MATH: |C| = 0.]

Therefore, only [MATH: |A|] and [MATH: |C|] are equal to [MATH: 0.]

---

Item 10 — Tutorial: Conditions When a Determinant Equals Zero

Content:
In conclusion, if an [MATH: n\!\times \!n] matrix [MATH: A] satisfies any one of the following conditions, then [MATH: \det(A)=0.]

Content:
1. [MATH: A] has a zero row/column
2. [MATH: A] has two identical rows/columns
3. [MATH: A] has two proportional rows/columns
4. [MATH: A] has a row/column that is a linear combination of other rows/columns

Content:
Notice that condition IV encompasses each of the conditions I, II, and III. If we have a zero row/column, two identical rows/columns, or proportional rows/columns, then the rows/columns form a linearly dependent set of vectors.
In turn, this means that one of the rows/columns is a linear combination of other rows/columns.

Content:
Watch out! While all of the above conditions are sufficient to conclude that [MATH: \det(A)=0,] only condition IV is necessary to conclude that [MATH: \det(A)=0.]
In other words, if we have a matrix [MATH: A] with [MATH: \det(A)=0,] then conditions I, II, and III may or may not be satisfied, while condition IV must be satisfied.

Content:
So, we have the following theorem:

Content:
> [MATH: \det(A)=0] if and only if one of the rows/columns of [MATH: A] is a linear combination of other rows/columns of [MATH: A.]

Content:
Finally, note also that in the case of a [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix only, statements III and IV mean the same thing.

---
